desc:
Given an integer array nums and two values minK ≤ maxK, return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays whose minimum equals minK and whose maximum equals maxK.

nums = [1, 3, 5, 2, 7, 5], minK = 1, maxK = 5
qualifying: [1,3,5] and [1,3,5,2]
result = 2
hints: Elements outside [minK, maxK] split the array into independent segments. Inside a segment, what still has to be checked?
A subarray whose elements all lie in [minK, maxK] has minimum exactly minK unless all its elements are > minK, and maximum exactly maxK unless all its elements are < maxK.
Let f(lo, hi) be the number of subarrays with every element in [lo, hi] (0 if lo > hi). Use inclusion-exclusion: f(minK, maxK) - f(minK+1, maxK) - f(minK, maxK-1) + f(minK+1, maxK-1).
editorial: Define f(lo, hi) = number of subarrays whose elements all lie in [lo, hi]; it is a sum of L(L+1)/2 over maximal runs of such elements, computed in one pass (add the current run length at every position). If lo > hi the range is empty and the count is 0.

Among subarrays inside [minK, maxK], those that fail the minimum condition have all elements in [minK+1, maxK], and those that fail the maximum condition have all elements in [minK, maxK-1]. The ones failing both lie in [minK+1, maxK-1]. By inclusion-exclusion the answer is f(minK, maxK) - f(minK+1, maxK) - f(minK, maxK-1) + f(minK+1, maxK-1).

This is the "at most" subtraction trick in two dimensions. When minK == maxK the last three terms are 0 and the answer is just the number of subarrays made of equal values minK. Four linear passes: O(n) time, O(1) space. (A single pass that tracks the last positions of minK, maxK and the last out-of-range element also works.)
